title: INTRODUCTION
content: “I thought they were crazy, rebuilding civilization on the exact place where the dragons had come down from the sky. Even if it had been over 200 years, everyone knows a dragon’s lifetime can be far longer than that. Yet, here I am like all the other fools. Driven by my thirst for fame and to fill my satchel with coin. I arrived at the same time as other risk-takers, lured by a chance for adventure and a desire to live a life that is more than normal. I have decided to make my way in this dangerous world...” Dragons Down is a board game set in a Western fantasy world. Players act as adventurers seeking fame and wealth, in the hope of becoming a legend. They will explore a devastated realm, search and loot hidden treasure sites looking for great treasures and epic artifacts, fulfill quests, cast magic, enchant the land, trade with the locals, and perform many heroic deeds. All of this while fighting or sneaking past savage monsters... and perhaps other adventurers too. The game is a giant sandbox that you can play in with your own goals in mind or choose to play one of the included scenarios. Be warned, you are about to enter a dangerous place, where riches and fame await the bold, but where one false step can be your last. Welcome to the world of Dragons Down.

title: SANDBOXES AND SCENARIOS
content: Dragons Down ships with various sandboxes and scenarios to provide many player options. We recommend starting with “Scenario 1: Entering Dragons Down” in the scenario book. Once comfortable with the game, choose another scenario or play using the Open Realm, Explore the Realm, or Legendary sandboxes below.

title: Open Realm Sandbox
content: Open Realm is the basic sandbox game mode of Dragons Down. Select any terrain packs you wish to use in this game session. It is recommended to include either the malevolent mountains or the cruel caves or both in your game session.

title: Map
content: Deal all tiles as evenly as possible to each player and then build the map starting with a random player and moving clockwise. Each player places one map tile, either side up. The placed map tile must touch two other tiles, if possible, and must connect to at least one existing path. All paths that touch a tile must match existing paths on those tiles.

title: Game Start
content: On their first turn of the game, heroes take a move action to enter the map from any path extending off the edge of the map.

title: Game Length
content: 30 turns

title: Victory Conditions
content: The hero with the most legend points at game end wins the game (even if deceased). Ties are broken by most fame, most epic treasures, most treasures, and then gold.

title: Explore the Realm Sandbox
content: Explore the Realm is identical to Open Realm except that the map is built during game play rather than created prior to game start.

title: Map
content: Place a random civilization tile belonging to a terrain pack in play in the center of the table. Place the tile’s civilization location and two random civilization tokens in the map tile. Then shuffle all remaining map tiles together to create a map tile stack.

title: Game Start
content: On their first turn, players place their hero on any clearing in the civilization map tile and then take their turn normally

title: Game Length
content: 30 turns

title: Victory Conditions
content: The hero with the most legend points at game end wins the game (even if deceased). Ties are broken by most fame, most epic treasures, most treasures, and then gold.

title: Additional Rules
content: Adds the Explore action, which is explained in the Actions section of the rules.

title: Legendary Sandbox
content: Perfect for solo play or for players who would rather play in a competitive way racing to a set number of LPs.

title: Map
content: Players may use the map rules for either Open Realm or Explore the Realm.

title: Game Start
content: Use the rules for either Open Realm or Explore the Realm.

title: Multi-player
content: Indefinite

title: Solo
content: 30 turns

title: Multi-player
content: 20 legend points (or any number agreed to by the players). The player who first retires with 20 legend points wins the game.

title: Solo
content: The player loses if they do not retire with 20 legend points before the game ends. Epic victory: Retire with 30 legend points.

title: SETUP
content: We recommend that you review the components section before actually setting up a game for play. Refer to this page when you are ready to set up a game.

title: Game Setup
content: White bubbles in the sample set up diagram Players decide which terrain packs they will use during this game session. The image to the right shows a sample setup for a game using the Malevolent Mountains and Cruel Caves terrain packs. 1. Place the terrain setup cards in play near the play area within easy reach of everyone, random side up (side 2 is slightly more difficult). Place the matching civilization cards, random side up, below the terrain setup cards. 2. For each terrain pack in play, shuffle the wilderness tokens and place the tokens face-down on the matching space on the terrain setup card. 3. Build a single civilization token pool by shuffling all of the civilization tokens for the terrain packs in play together and place them in a face-down pile near the terrain setup cards. 4. Build a single treasure site pool by shuffling all of the treasure site tokens for terrain packs in play together and place them in a face-down pile near the terrain setup cards. 5. Build a single mission deck by shuffling together all mission cards for terrain packs in play (there is a terrain pack icon on the front face of each mission card). Place the mission deck face-down near the terrain setup cards. 6. Separately shuffle the spell (not the hero starting spells), treasure, and deep treasure cards and place them in face-down piles near the terrain setup cards. 7. Monsters: There should be no setup required for the monster counters. Set the monster tray near the play areas within easy reach of all players. 8. Place the legend, fame, and gold tokens in separate piles near the map to form a pool of tokens. 9. Shuffle all of the map tiles for the terrain packs in play. Then follow the instructions on building the map for the scenario/game mode being played. The image to the right shows the map when playing with Open Realm rules where the map is built prior to the start of game play. 10. When a civilization map tile is revealed, roll a d6 and place the corresponding civilization location in the matching clearing. Reroll any 5s or 6s. Take the natives listed on the terrain setup card and stack them on the civilization location in any order.

title: Hero Selection
content: Black bubbles in the sample set up diagram Players now select the hero that they wish to play. Each combination of lineage and class cards produces a unique hero. The order of hero selection is determined randomly, but can most often be done simultaneously. 1. Each player places a hero board in front of them. 2. Each player chooses one lineage card (dwarf, elf, halfling, or human) and one class card (numerous choices). The two cards are placed side-by-side on their hero board, either side up, to create their hero. The hero has the capabilities shown on the combination of lineage and class cards. Take the matching hero counter and targeting token for the selected class as well. 3. Health. The hero takes a number of heart tokens equal to the number of hearts shown on both cards. Place these hearts in the healthy box on the hero board. 4. Action cubes: Each player takes a number of action cubes that match the color of the cubes shown on their lineage and class cards and places them in their healthy box on their hero board. If a cube shows two or more colors, the player has the option of taking any matching cube color shown. E.g. if the cube is black and purple, the player may take either a black cube or a purple cube. 5. Each player takes the equipment listed on their face-up class card from the item cards and places them in the appropriate matching locations on their hero board (e.g. helmet in the head location). 6. Each player takes their starting gold and places it in their backpack. 7. If the hero has starting spells listed on the class card, the player selects spells from the Hero Starting Spells card deck. A. Players may only select spells of a color that match one or more of their starting magic cube colors. B. Once all players have selected their starting spells, place them below the hero board (starting spells may be kept secret until used, if players wish) and place all remaining hero starting spell cards back in the box. They will not be used in this game session. 8. Once all heroes have their starting equipment, shuffle the remaining item cards and place them in a single face-down pile near the setup cards.

title: You are now ready to play Dragons Down.
Dice
content: Dragons Down uses custom dice to determine the outcome of some events. Golden Rule: In Dragons Down players roll two dice and take the least favorable result of the die facings unless otherwise noted. Dice results are explained in the relevant sections of these rules and are listed here for completeness.

title: Summoning Dice
content: Four dice are rolled during the Monster Activation step of the Battle phase. The dice come in two colors: Gray (wandering monster dice) and Black (local monster dice). Each color has two dice; one with symbols that summon monsters and one with numbers that show the number of summoned monsters that will appear. The wandering monster dice summon monsters that are unique to a terrain pack (e.g. juvenile dragons in the malevolent mountains). Wandering monsters for each terrain are shown on the bottom left of the map tiles from that terrain pack. The local monster dice summon the local monsters and treasure site guardians. The faces of the local monster die show either a treasure site symbol or the various symbols shown on the bottom right of the map tiles. Monster summoning is explained later in these rules.

title: Search Dice
content: Two dice are rolled when a hero attempts to find a treasure site or hidden path. Each die has 3 spyglass facings (success) and three blank facings (failure).

title: Hit Dice
content: Two dice are rolled during combat resolution when an attack speed is less than or equal to a maneuver speed (and thus, not an automatic hit). Each die has 3 hit facings (success), 1 hit if equal facing (possible success), and 2 blank facings (failure).

title: Ranged Attack Dice
content: Two dice are rolled after a ranged attack hits (bow, crossbow, thrown dagger, spear, etc., spells such as fireball, thrown explosive potion, etc.). The facings of each ranged die either increase or decrease the amount of damage delivered during a successful ranged attack.

title: Monster Dice
content: Two monster dice are rolled whenever a hero attempts to hide, when monsters are in combat and may change tactics, and when a hero with outlaw tokens dies or retires from the game. Each die has 2 monster symbols and 4 blank facings. Monster die results are explained later in these rules.

title: Loot Dice
content: Two dice are rolled whenever a hero attempts to loot a found treasure site. Each facing shows a number 1 through 5 and one facing shows a grabby hand. A hero that rolls two grabby hands may select a treasure using special rules explained later.

title: Haggle Dice
content: Two dice are rolled when a hero attempts to lower the price to buy merchandise from a merchant. The base price of merchandise is 3x the printed price. Each haggle die has a number 0 through 4 (various levels of success) and a door closed symbol (failure).

title: Mission Dice
content: A number of dice equal to the number of matching attribute symbols on a hero’s card are rolled as bonus rewards for completing missions. Each mission die facing shows a gold or fame reward that is earned by the hero in addition to the printed rewards on the mission card.

title: Learn Spells Dice
content: Two dice are rolled when attempting to learn a new spell. Unlucky heroes may become cursed while attempting to learn spells. Each learn spells die has three book facings (success), two blank facings (no effect), and one curse facing (cursed).

title: Legend Points
content: Unless specified in the scenario rules, legend points (LPs) are the victory points of Dragons Down. LPs represent being remembered far beyond your lifetime. LPs are not limited by the quantities provided.

title: Fame
content: Heroes also earn fame during game play. Fame represents the more temporary aspects of being remembered. Being famous in your lifetime is different than being a legend. Some of a hero’s accumulated fame disappears if that hero dies. Fame is not limited by the quantities provided.

title: Gold
content: Gold is the currency of the realm and is used to purchase various equipment, spells, and cures used by heroes. Gold is not limited by the quantities provided.

title: Terrain Packs
content: Included with Dragons Down are multiple terrain packs: the cruel caves, malevolent mountains, and wicked woods. Each terrain pack has its own setup card, map tiles, map tokens, civilization location and natives, monsters, treasure sites, guardians, merchants, and missions. Additional terrain packs are available to expand your gaming experience. Players may tailor their game experience for the depth and length of game session they desire by including or excluding terrain packs as they wish.

title: Terrain Setup Cards
content: Only use setup cards for terrain packs in play. Setup cards show tokens, natives, treasures sites, guardians, and merchants associated with the terrain. Some terrain setup cards have a red arrow pointing to the guardian location, which indicates that the guardian can be summoned to locations in more than one terrain setup card (in the Dragons Down: Desolation expansion).

title: Map Tiles
content: Each terrain pack has one civilization tile and five wilderness tiles, which are used to create a unique map for each game. Wilderness map tiles have six circular clearings while civilization tiles have four clearings. Heroes, monsters, treasure sites, etc., exist in clearings. Clearing types included in the game are plains (white), caves (black), mountains (red), woods (green), and swamps (yellow). Connecting these clearings are paths and hidden paths. The components of each terrain pack have a common theme. However, the clearings on map tiles are not all the same, and will feature other terrain types. Example: the tile shown is from the caves terrain pack, but clearing 1 is a woods clearing and clearing 3 is a plains clearing. The color, name, and symbol on the map tile shows the terrain pack it is from. Each wilderness map tile has summoning icons, which determine which monsters are summoned to the map tile. Civilization map tiles do not summon monsters.

title: Monsters
content: Monsters in Dragons Down can be regular monsters (e.g. Giant Spiders) or guardians of treasure sites (e.g. Great Drake). Regular monsters are listed on map tiles. Guardians are listed on the terrain setup cards next to the treasure site they protect. All monsters should remain in the plastic insert until summoned onto the map.

title: Civilization Locations
content: Civilization locations represent various places where humanity has repopulated the realm. When a civilization map tile is placed, roll a d6 and place the matching location, and natives listed on the terrain pack setup card, in the indicated clearing (if there is no match, reroll the die).

title: Natives
content: All civilization locations have a population of humanoids that live there which is shown on the terrain setup cards. Natives are placed on their starting civilization locations once the matching location is placed on the map.

title: Civilization Tokens
content: Civilization tokens are placed in civilized map tiles when they are explored by a hero. They represent the various merchants of the realm and offer the heroes a place to buy additional equipment, sell the treasures that they loot from treasure sites, and accept valuable missions.

title: Civilization Cards and Titles
content: Gold does not directly contribute to victory in Dragons Down. Heroes may spend gold and/or satisfy prerequisites on civilization cards at civilization locations to claim titles to earn legend points and fame. These cards are double-sided to increase replayability.

title: Mission Cards
content: Heroes may accept missions from merchants at civilization locations. Missions are organized into Atrocities (red banner), Quests (white banner), and Expeditions (brown banner). Missions are a good way to earn legend points, fame, and gold... as well as infamy or redemption.

title: Wilderness Tokens
content: Wilderness tokens are placed in wilderness tiles. The back of wilderness tokens shows the terrain pack to which it belongs, which also determines what type of tile it is placed in (e.g. cave wilderness tokens are placed in cave tiles). On the front of wilderness tokens are either treasure site locations, magic gates to teleport around the realm, special locations, or other game effects on the tokens.

title: Treasure Site Tokens
content: Treasure site tokens have a map scroll with the word “Site” on the back. On the front of the token is a symbol showing to which terrain pack the site belongs. When a wilderness token is revealed with a treasure site location on it, a random treasure site token is drawn and placed in the tile .

title: Hero Cards
content: Players will play the role of a hero created by the combination of a lineage card and a class card. The hero has the combined characteristics of both cards: • Two special advantages (one on each card). • Attributes: Cunning, wisdom, and charisma (for interactions with civilization such as haggling and completing missions). • Health. How hard can this hero get hit without dying. • Attack speed. How fast can this hero potentially attack. • Maneuver speed. How fast can this hero potentially dodge attacks. • Aim boxes (only used if playing with the optional Player vs. Player rules). • Starting action cubes and equipment for the hero.

title: Item and Treasure Cards
content: Item and treasure cards are the principal equipment, and means of survival, for heroes in Dragons Down. • Items are indicated by a wooden plank for a banner on the card (e.g. Plate Armor). • Treasures are indicated by a brown cloth banner on the card (e.g. Warblade and Spell Scroll). • Epic treasures, the most valuable treasures in the game, are indicated by a red cloth banner on the card (e.g. Magical Bowl of Mixing). Additional information on the cards show the effects of the card and where on the hero’s body the card is equipped when active. All of this is explained in detail later in these rules.

title: Spells
content: Dragons Down is a world full of magic. Heroes can enchant the land, cast spells, learn new spells, and buy spells from merchants. The layout of spell cards is very similar to the layout of item and treasure cards, but adds some additional information like duration, targeting, and magic cube requirements. Spells are explained in detail later in these rules.

title: Hero Board
content: The hero board is a representation of the hero, their status, and their equipment. The player places their lineage and class cards together to form their hero, their action cubes and health hearts in the healthy box, inactive cards face- down in the backpack and active cards face-up in the locations that match the card’s location symbols. Spells are placed underneath the hero board. Cubes and hearts in the healthy box are considered healthy (usable). Over the course of the game, a hero’s cubes and hearts may be moved to the wounded box to show that those cubes and hearts are wounded (unusable). The top of the hero board shows the various actions a hero may take during their action phase. The Black arrow in the upper left is the symbol for all actions. The symbol for each individual action is shown next to its description.

title: Hero Counters and Outlaw Tokens
content: Heroes are represented by blue-ringed counters with the symbol of their hero class in the middle of the counter. In addition, each hero has a matching targeting token that is used to determine player order and to mark the target that a hero is attacking with a spell or weapon during combat. Heroes receive outlaw tokens when they complete atrocity missions or assault other heroes and natives of the realm.

title: Cubes
content: During combat, players will place action cubes on their lineage cards, class cards, items, treasures, and spells in order to attack and survive attacks against them.

title: Action Cubes
content: Action Cubes come in 3 different types: Might Cubes: Might cubes are red and signify how much strength a hero is using in an attack. Most often, might cubes are placed on weapons in order to cause damage to monsters in the game. Speed Cubes: Speed cubes are brown and signify how much effort the hero is putting into the speed of an attack or the speed of their maneuver to dodge an attack made against them. Magic cubes: Magic cubes are black, blue, gray, green, purple, white, and yellow. They represent specialized knowledge possessed by the hero and are only placed on spells cards and some treasures in order to power them for use.

title: Status Cubes
content: Status cubes are pink and track wounds on monsters and the status of heroes who have sneaked, made noise, alerted, and/or successfully hidden this turn.

title: Health Hearts
content: Health Hearts represent the life force of a hero. If a hero ever has no hearts in their healthy box, they immediately die. Health Hearts are considered cubes for all purposes.

title: Reference Cards
content: Included with the game are reference cards that show how heroes earn legend points (LPs) and fame in the game.

title: Curses
content: The reverse side of the reference cards show the curse table to be used whenever a hero receives a curse. Curses are not cumulative. If a hero receives a curse they already have, ignore that curse die roll. Mark a hero’s curses with status cubes.

title: GAME PLAY
content: Each turn in the game is broken into an action phase and a battle phase.

title: Action Phase
content: 1. Turn Start: All heroes clear their statuses and become unblocked. 2. Actions: a. Determine the active hero. b. Active hero performs all of their actions. c. Repeat until all heroes have taken a turn.

title: Battle Phase
content: 1. Monster Activation: Monsters may move and be summoned. 2. Combat: Players cast spells and/or participate in combat.

title: Turn Start
content: All heroes clear their hidden, alerted, sneak, and make noise statuses. Remove any pink cubes from the upper portion of all hero boards. All heroes become unblocked. Flip all hero counters to their unblocked sides.

title: Actions
content: Mix all heroes’ targeting tokens together and randomly draw one to determine a start player for the turn. The start player performs all of their actions for the turn. Then draw a new token to determine the next player to perform their actions until all players have taken a turn. Players may perform up to 4 actions during their turn. Actions can be taken in any order and the same action may be taken any number of times. Caves If a hero begins their turn in a cave clearing, or enters a cave clearing during their turn, the hero loses one total action that turn (may use 3 actions instead of 4). A hero may not use a 4th action to enter a cave clearing. Monster Block Monsters block the active, unhidden hero if they are in the same clearing at the end of any action. The hero may attempt to hide to avoid being blocked (see Reactions on page 13). Blocked heroes are unhidden and lose all remaining actions and reactions until the end of the turn. Flip the hero counter over to its blocked side to denote that the hero is blocked.

title: The actions:
content: Alert The alert action allows a hero to unequip and equip any/all of their possessions (see Equipping on page 21 for full details). Additionally, during combat this turn the hero may use +1 speed cube during each round of combat. Place a pink status cube in the Alert box on the hero’s player board to indicate that the hero alerted this turn. Sneak - or- Make Noise The Sneak action improves the odds of a hero successfully hiding. Place a pink status cube in the Sneak box on the hero board when a hero takes a Sneak action. Heroes that sneak may ignore one failure die result (but, not two failures) during all hide reactions this turn (see Reactions on page 13). A hero may instead choose to Make Noise. They immediately become unhidden and are blocked if monsters are present. A hero may not Sneak and Make Noise in the same turn. Place a pink status cube in the Make Noise box on the hero board. After monster activation, but before combat, roll the summoning dice again for each hero that made noise this turn. Apply the results only to the clearing containing the hero rolling the dice using normal summoning rules, ignoring heroes in all other clearings in the tile. Move The Move action allows a hero to move to an adjacent clearing connected to the current clearing by a path, a gate, or a discovered hidden path. When a hidden hero moves to a new clearing, they lose any hidden status. The move costs one action except for the situations as explained below: Mountains or Swamps: A move action made into a mountain or swamp clearing requires +1 action cost. Gates: Once more than one gate is revealed, a hero may travel between any two gates as if they were connected by a path. The type of clearing being entered determines the movement cost to use the gate. Evading: Heroes that evaded during combat on the prior turn must spend their first action moving to an adjacent clearing. Heroes that evaded out of a cave clearing still lose one action that turn even if evading in the direction of a non-cave clearing. Place Tokens: When a hero enters a map tile that does not contain a treasure site, civilization, or wilderness token, place tokens in the tile. Exception: If a hero enters a new tile due to a spell effect during combat, reveal tokens once all combat is completed for the turn. Civilization tiles: Draw two random civilization tokens from the civilization token pile and reveal them in the civilization location clearing on the map tile. Fill any newly revealed merchants with the number of treasures, items, and missions indicated on the terrain setup card for that merchant. These cards are taken from the piles shuffled during game setup. The order of these cards does not matter. Wilderness tiles: Draw one random wilderness token from the matching terrain setup card and reveal it anywhere in the tile. Follow the instructions for the token drawn below. • Site: Draw a random site token from the site token pile. Place the treasure site in the clearing on the map tile indicated by number on the site token. • Numbered Token: Place the token in the clearing indicated by the number on the wilderness token. • Item: Draw an item from the top of the item pile. The hero may equip the card immediately (see Equipping on page 21). • Treasure: Draw a treasure from the top of the treasure pile (not the deep treasure pile). The hero may equip the card immediately (see Equipping on page 21). • Discovery: The hero rolls two mission dice and receives the rewards indicated by the dice roll. • Forgotten City/Dwarven Ruins: Reveal one additional token from each terrain setup card, repeating the above steps for each new token. The revealing hero receives 1 LP and 5 fame. Search When a hero searches, they select one of two options: 1. They may search for a hidden path that is connected to the clearing. 2. They may search for a treasure site in the clearing. The player rolls the two search dice. If the result shows two spyglasses, the hero has found the treasure site or hidden path. Any other result is a failure. Rerolls: If the hero chooses to search for the same target using consecutive search actions on the same turn, they only reroll search dice showing a blank result. When a hidden path is discovered, that hero may use the path during a move action as if it was a regular path for the rest of the game. When a treasure site is discovered for the first time, two things occur: 1. The hero gains legend points (LPs) and fame for being the first to discover the site as shown on the player reference cards. 2. Draw a number of treasures and deep treasures from the appropriate piles as listed on the matching treasure site on the terrain setup card. Place the treasure cards on the treasure site location on the terrain setup card. Place the deep treasures on top of the treasure cards. Loot Once a player has found a treasure site, they may loot it using a loot action. A hero may not loot a treasure site that they have not discovered, even if it has been discovered by other heroes. Roll the two loot dice. If the player rolls only grabby hand icons, they may look at the top three treasures and keep one of them, returning the other two to the treasure pile in the original order. Otherwise, use the highest numeric die result for the loot roll result. Take the card from the treasure pile that is in the position of the loot roll result, counting from the top, or take no card if there are fewer cards in the treasure pile than the loot roll result. When a hero loots a treasure card they look at it secretly and decide whether they want to equip the card (place it face-up in a valid equipment location) or whether they want to place it face-down in their backpack (see Equipping on page 21). Exception: treasure cards with a red location symbol must always be face-up regardless of their location. A player may reveal cards in their backpack at any time. When an epic treasure card (with a red banner) is possessed and revealed for the first time, the revealing player earns LPs and fame as indicated on the player reference card. Rewards for epic treasures only occur once per game per epic treasure. Learn The learn action allows a hero to attempt to learn a spell attached to a spell book or spell scroll they possess. A hero must possess a magic cube that matches the spell type of the spell (healthy or wounded). Roll the two learn spell dice. • If both sides show a spell book, the hero learns the spell and removes it from the spell book or spell scroll and places it in the known spells location on their hero board. They earn the LPs and fame shown on the player reference cards. If the last spell is removed from a treasure card, remove the treasure card from the game. • If the dice show one or more curse symbols, the hero fails and receives one curse. Roll on the curse table immediately and apply the effects until the curse is removed. The curse table is shown on the back side of the reference cards. • In any other situation, the learn spells action has no effect. Rerolls: If the hero chooses to learn the same spell using consecutive learn actions on the same turn, they only reroll learn dice showing a blank or curse result. Rest A hero may become wounded for a variety of reasons. In order to move cubes from the wounded box to the healthy box, the hero must rest. A hero may take a quick rest, a short rest, or a long rest, moving one, two, and three cubes from the wounded box to the healthy box for a cost of two, three, and four actions respectively. Trade A hero may perform a trade action to swap with another hero, do commerce, complete missions, claim titles, or remove curses and spells. A single trade action may only do one of the following things: 1. Swap: Swap any number of item cards, treasure cards, gold, or the location of treasure sites or hidden paths in the current clearing with one other unhidden, unblocked hero that is in the clearing. Spells and missions may not be swapped. 2. Commerce: Buy cards, sell cards, and/or take missions from a merchant in the same clearing. Each step below may be performed once in a single trade action and in any order. • Look: Look at all cards on the terrain setup card for one merchant that is in the clearing. • Sell: The hero may sell any number of items or treasures from their hero board for the listed price. Spells may not be sold unless attached to a spell book or scroll (see page 29 for the sale price of a spell book or spell scroll). Place these sold items with the merchant. They are immediately available for sale to any hero. • Buy: Buy one item for 3x the price shown on the card (see page 29 for the purchase price of a spell book or spell scroll). • If the hero cannot, or does not want to, pay the full price, they may haggle over the price (see Haggling on page 21). • When purchasing an item or treasure, the hero may equip it immediately (see Equipping on page 21). • When an epic treasure card (with a red banner) is purchased, the hero may reveal the treasure to earn LPs and fame as indicated on the player reference card, if the treasure was not already revealed this game. • Take Missions: Take 0, 1, or 2 mission cards from the merchant and place it face-down in the hero’s backpack. A hero may keep a maximum of two uncompleted mission cards in their possession at the end of their turn; discard any excess. Missions are refilled at the end of the player’s turn (after all actions) so all merchants have their maximum number of listed missions available. If the mission deck is empty, reshuffle the missions discard pile and recreate. If none, the merchants do not restock missions. • Repair: A merchant will repair any number of damaged armor cards if the hero pays the price shown on the damaged armor card. Discard the gold to the pool and remove any pink status cube on the armor. 3. Complete a Mission: All missions require that players perform a trade action at a certain location to claim the mission reward. Remove completed missions from the game. (see page 23 for more information on Missions). 4. Claim a Title: If a hero meets the prerequisites on the matching civilization card, and a member of that native group is present, they may place one pink status cube on a title, pay the price listed, and receive the rewards shown on the card. Small boxes may only be claimed once. Large boxes may be claimed an unlimited number of times (one per trade action). 5. Remove Curses and Spells: A hero in a civilization location may remove any number of curses and permanent spells from a willing hero in the clearing for a cost of 5 gold per curse or permanent spell dispelled. Enchant Tile If a hero has a colored magic cube and spends 3 consecutive actions enchanting in a single turn, this happens: • The tile in which they are located is flipped over to the opposite side. The name of the tile should be placed so that it matches the previous orientation. All counters and tokens are placed in the same clearings in which they existed before the flip. • The player removes any magic cubes that are on the tile and returns them to the pool. The player places one magic cube from the pool matching a magic cube they possess (even if in the wounded box) and places it on the tile. Any permanent spells that match the color of the cube in a tile are activated immediately anytime the affected hero is in the tile. Additionally, casting a spell that requires a color that matches the cube in the tile requires one less magic cube to cast (see Spells on page 22). Explore [Only used with the Exploration rules] A hero that is in a clearing with a path leading directly to a map edge may explore the adjacent tile. When a hero performs an explore action, select a connected path leading off the map and take a map tile from the bottom of the map tile stack and place it connected to the path. The player may choose any orientation and may place either side of the tile face-up. However, all existing paths on adjacent map tiles must connect to paths on the placed tile. The tile must be placed, if possible. If there is no legal placement, the action is forfeited and the tile is placed on the top of the map tile stack. After placing the tile, the hero may then move into a connected clearing on the explored tile, spending any extra action cost if moving into a mountain or swamp clearing. Mountain Exploration: If a player is in a mountain clearing, they may explore an adjacent empty map tile location. The map tile is placed using the explore rules above. The map tile must connect to at least one path on any tile. Pass The hero’s action phase ends.

title: Reactions
content: Reactions are special actions that can only be taken when certain circumstances are met, and they can be taken out of turn or even out of the action phase. Every reaction defines one or more trigger conditions, and every time a trigger condition is met the player may carry out the reaction once. Hide Triggers: An unblocked hero may make a Hide reaction and gain the hide status when any of the following occurs: • A monster blocks a hero during the Action Phase. • At the end of Monster Activation. • During the Cleanup step if the hero ambushed this combat round. The Hide reaction is free (does not count as an action). Roll the two monster dice. If a monster symbol is rolled on either of the dice, the Hide action fails and the block is successful. If there are no monster symbols in the roll result, the hero gains the hidden status and the block has no effect. Place a pink cube on the hidden box on the hero board. If the hero took the Sneak action this turn they may ignore one monster symbol when determining success or failure. Once a hero is hidden, they remain hidden until they move to a new clearing, take the make noise action, choose to become unhidden, ambush, or a new turn starts.

title: Player Turn End
content: Once the hero has completed all of their desired actions for their turn, play passes to the next player. Once all players have performed all their actions, the action phase ends and the Battle Phase begins.

title: Monster Activation
content: The start player rolls all 4 summoning dice. One Gray die (wandering monsters) and one Black die (local monsters) have symbols matching the icons on the bottom of the map tiles. The other dice contain numbers showing how many monsters arrive if monsters are summoned. Process the Gray dice first, then the Black dice. Return Arrow: If the arrow symbol is rolled on one of the dice do the following: • Monsters Return: Return all monsters in map tiles containing no heroes to the monster tray. • Monsters Move: Monsters in a clearing with a hero do not move. All other monsters that are on the map tile are moved to the clearing of the hero on the map tile that is closest to the start player in turn order. Summoning symbol: If the symbol on either of the dice matches a summoning symbol on a map tile containing a hero, the following occurs in order: 1. Monsters Move: Monsters in a clearing with a hero do not move. All other monsters that are on the map tile are moved to the clearing of the hero that is closest to the start player in turn order. 2. Monsters Summon: The monster type shown on the map tile next to the summoning symbol will summon from the monster tray to the map tile. If more than one hero is in the tile, monsters are summoned in each clearing starting with the player closest to the start player in turn order. Each clearing summons only once regardless of the number of heroes there. The number of monsters summoned is equal to the number shown on the die that matches the color of the symbol die. Randomly select that many matching monsters from the monster tray and place them in the clearing with the hero. If there are not enough monsters, summon what remains. Note: If the monster listed on the map tile has a dual dice icon beside the monster symbol, then the number of monsters summoned to the tile is the sum of both numbered summoning dice. Treasure Site Symbol: If the treasure site symbol is rolled on one of the dice and a map tile contains one or more heroes and one or more treasure sites then guardians are summoned. Move all guardians from wherever they are located to the clearing containing the matching treasure site for that guardian, even if that causes the guardian to leave a clearing containing a hero, another map tile, or the monster tray. Moved and summoned monsters are always placed name-side up. In player order, each hero that made noise this turn rolls all of the summoning dice again and applies the results to their clearing only. Unblocked heroes may wish to take a hide reaction at the end of Monster Activation. Hide reactions are important only when a monster, native, or another hero is in the clearing (if playing with the optional Player vs. Player rules).

title: Monster Activation
content: The enchanter is the first player, followed by the sorcerer, barbarian, cleric, and druid. The enchanter rolls the summoning dice resulting in a claw symbol for the local monster die, a malevolent mountain symbol for the wandering monster die, and a 1 for both numbered dice. Enchanter’s (and sorcerer’s) map tile The local monster die matches the claw symbol on the Secret Dens. 1. Monster Move: No movement since no monsters are present. 2. Monster Summon: The goblins have the dual dice icon next to their symbol, so the number of goblins summoned is equal to the sum of the two dice, two goblins (red arrow). First, two goblins are summoned to the clearing with the enchanter because the enchanter was before the sorcerer in turn order. Second, two goblins are summoned to the sorcerer’s clearing (if any goblins remain). Barbarian’s map tile Both dice match the symbols on the Lonely Mountains map tile. 1. Monster Move: The griffon already in the Lonely Mountains map tile moves to the barbarian’s clearing (yellow arrow). 2. Monster Summon: The monsters for the Lonely Mountains are griffons and juvenile dragons. Neither has the dual dice icon next to their symbol, so one of each is summoned to the barbarian’s clearing (red arrow). Cleric’s map tile The wandering monster die matches the symbol on the Tri-Peaks tile. 3. Monster Move: The juvenile dragon already in the Tri-Peaks map tile moves to the clearing of the cleric (yellow arrow). 4. Monster Summon: The symbol summons Juvenile Dragons to the Tri- Peaks tile. Since they do not have dual dice icon next to their symbol, one Juvenile Dragon is summoned to the cleric’s clearing (red arrow). Druid’s map tile There are no dice symbols that match the symbols in the druid’s map tile so no monsters move or summon in that map tile.

title: Combat
content: Combat is completed for each clearing containing one or more heroes beginning with the clearing of the start player and proceeding in turn order. Clearings without heroes are ignored. Most often, combat can be done simultaneously for all clearings. Combat occurs even if no monsters are present. This allows heroes to cast spells and perform the cleanup step of combat even if alone in a clearing.

title: Ambush
content: Hidden heroes may not do the target, hero tactics, or resolve steps of combat explained below unless armed with a ranged weapon or casting a spell. Using a ranged weapon or casting a spell from hiding is called an ambush. All combat rules apply except that monsters may not target the ambusher while hidden.

title: Combat Steps
content: The combat steps in each clearing are as follows. Should it matter, all steps are done in player turn order. Each circuit through these steps is called a combat round: 1. Challenge: In player order, hidden heroes may choose to become unhidden. Then, each monster challenges a random unhidden hero or monster controlled by a hero, in the clearing. • Multiple monsters may challenge a single hero, even if other heroes are not challenged by a monster. • Monsters challenge heroes that are shape shifted into monsters. • Monsters under the control of a hero (e.g. elementals) are considered heroes for all purposes during combat. • Monsters do not challenge natives, and vice versa. They ignore one another. 2. Activation: A hero under the effects of an inactive permanent spell may move a magic cube matching the color of the spell type from their healthy box to their wounded box to cause the spell to take effect immediately. Spells are explained on page 22 of these rules. • If a hero is in a map tile that is enchanted with a magic cube matching the color of a permanent spell, this happens automatically without wounding a magic cube. • A hero may not wound a cube to activate an inactive permanent spell that is affecting another hero. 3. Evade: In player order, heroes may evade combat if they can place more brown speed cubes in their maneuver speed boxes than the highest single maneuver speed of all monsters that are challenging them. • If the player cannot place enough brown speed cubes in the maneuver speed boxes, the hero may not evade combat. • Heroes that evade take no further part in combat and are placed on a path leading out of the clearing of the player’s choice (not a gate). Next turn, they must move as their first action. Return the cubes to their healthy box. • Evaded monsters do not challenge other heroes this combat round. 4. Target: Heroes, and then monsters, choose a target for this combat round. • Monsters always target the hero they are challenging. • In player order, each hero in the clearing selects a monster to target. Place the hero’s target token on the monster they are attacking. Multiple heroes may attack the same monster. • When targeting with a controlled monster, the hero selects which side of the monster chip to place face-up. It will not change during monster tactics. • If a monster was evaded by the hero they challenged, the monster attacks no one, but may still be targeted by an attack from another hero. • A hero may target themselves or another hero if casting a spell. 5. Hero Tactics: In secret, each hero places their action cubes on the boxes for their might, spells, attack speed and/or maneuver speed. • A hero may place up to 5 action cubes on their boxes. The action cube limit is +1 speed cube if the hero performed an alert action during the action phase this turn. • Might (red) cubes may only be placed on might (red) boxes. This represents the strength that the hero is putting into the attack. • Speed (brown) cubes may only be placed on attack speed and/or maneuver speed boxes (both brown). This represents the speed of the hero’s attack and maneuver. An attack or maneuver speed of 0 or less is still an attack and/or maneuver. • Magic cubes may only be placed on boxes that match the color of the cube being placed. Note that some boxes accept any color of magic cube. • Each combat round, a hero may only use one card that casts a spell or causes an attack to occur. A hero may place additional cubes on other treasure cards, if they wish. A hero may always place cubes on their lineage and class cards. • A hero may not place cubes on possessions in their backpack. • If a hero is placing cubes on a card, they must fill all dark red or dark brown (mandatory) boxes on the card. They do not have to place cubes in the light red or light brown (optional) boxes on a card. • If the hero is casting a spell, all boxes on the spell card must be filled with 1 cube of the matching color. Multi-color boxes may contain any color of magic cube. If the map tile is enchanted, any one box matching the enchanting color does not need to be filled. • Once all players have placed their action cubes, reveal all placements. 6. Monster Tactics: For each uncontrolled monster in the clearing, roll one monster die. If it shows a monster symbol, flip the monster counter over. These are the new characteristics of the monster for this round of combat. At the end of monster tactics, if a monster’s tactics are an attack with multiple targets (e.g. fireball), the monster will add random additional heroes as targets, in addition to the hero they originally targeted. 7. Resolve: Process all attacks in attack speed order and fully resolve one attack before proceeding to the next. A. Attack Order: Starting with the fastest unresolved attack speed, regardless if it is a spell or a weapon, process the attack. • Ties for attack speed are broken by the attack length shown on each weapon or spell card (the number on top of a sword icon). • The attack length of monsters is shown as a red number above the attack speed on the counter. No number indicates an attack length of 0. • Tied attack speeds and attack lengths strike simultaneously. If spell resolution order matters, break ties randomly. B. Attack Resolution: For each attack in order, perform the following steps. • If the attacker’s attack speed is faster than the target’s maneuver speed, the attack hits. Otherwise, roll the two hit dice. • If either die is blank: The attack misses. • If both dice are hit symbols: The attack hits. • If the dice are a combination of hits and equal signs: The attack hits if the attacker’s attack speed is equal to the maneuver speed of the target. Otherwise, it misses. C. Damage: If the attack misses, ignore this step; proceed to step D. Golden Rule of Damage: Any time a target is hit by an attack with an actual damage one or more, it will either be killed or take one wound. Attacks with an actual damage of less than one have no effect and are ignored. • If the attack is a spell, apply the effects of the spell as printed on the card. Spells are explained on page 22 of these rules. • If a weapon, count the number of cubes on the weapon card or the number printed on the red cube on the monster counter. Add to this damage the number of sword icons covered by cubes on the weapon card or printed on the monster counter. This is the base damage. • A monster or native is armored if there is a shield icon on the counter. A hero may choose whether an attack on them hits their head or torso. A hero is armored if they have an armor card on their hero board in the slot being hit. If the hero has a shield in a weapon slot, they may choose if they want to use the shield as armor for the attack. A hero must choose which armor to use, if any, before ranged attack dice rolls. • If the attack has one or more sword icons on it and the target is armored, reduce the base damage by one. • If the attack is a ranged attack (arrow symbol on the monster, weapon, or spell), the attacking hero rolls the two ranged attack dice and adjusts the base damage by the worst result shown. • This is the actual damage. Ignore all attacks with an actual damage that is less than one. • The target is a monster: • If the actual damage is greater than or equal to monster’s health, the monster is killed. • Monster health: Health is the printed health value on top of a heart/shield/undead symbol on the counter, minus any wounds on the counter (see Wounds on page 17). • If the actual damage is less than the monster’s health, the monster takes one wound (see Wounds on page 17). • The target is a hero using armor: • If the actual damage is higher than the number in the shield icon of the armor card, the armor is destroyed and removed from the game. The hero takes one wound (see Wounds on page 17). • If the actual damage is equal to the number in the shield icon of the armor card, the armor is damaged. Place a pink status cube on the armor card. If the armor already has a pink cube on it, it is destroyed. The hero takes one wound. • If the actual damage is greater than zero, but less than the number on the shield icon of the armor card, the armor is not damaged or destroyed. The hero takes one wound. • The target is a hero not using armor: • If the actual damage is greater than or equal to the hero’s health, the hero is killed. • Hero health: A hero’s health is equal to the number of hearts in the hero’s healthy box. Hearts in the wounded box and action cubes anywhere have no impact on health. • If the actual damage is less than the health of the hero, the hero takes one wound. D. Repeat step 7: Resolve the next attack in attack speed order until all attacks have been resolved for the combat round. 8. Cleanup: A quick end-of-round clean-up step occurs. • Adjust Equipment: A hero that did not cast a spell or use an item or treasure this combat round may unequip one card and then equip one card. This card may be the same card (see Equipping on page 21). • Rearm: A hero that threw a melee/ranged weapon may equip one card from their backpack to the vacated weapon location on their hero board. • Hide: If a hidden hero cast a spell or used an item or treasure this combat round, they must roll to stay hidden. Heroes that fail to hide are unhidden for all purposes for the remainder of combat. Note: Heroes that performed a sneak action this turn may not ignore any monster symbol results on this hide attempt. The halfling’s lineage advantage may not be used to reroll a monster die. • Spells Wound: If a hero cast a spell with a cube in a spell box containing a wound symbol, that cube is moved to the wounded box for that hero. • All remaining action cubes are placed in the hero’s healthy box. • If two consecutive rounds of combat occur without any hero or monster taking a wound or dying, combat ends in the clearing for the turn. Otherwise, proceed to step 1 of combat and repeat these steps.

title: Wounds
content: When a monster is wounded, place a pink cube on the monster counter to signify that its health is lower than its printed health. A monster may have multiple pink cubes to show multiple wounds. Each wound cube lowers the monster’s health by one. When a hero is wounded, the hero must immediately move a cube or heart to the wounded box from the hero’s healthy box, lineage card, class card, weapon card, a treasure card, or a spell card. A hero with no hearts in their healthy box is killed. If a wound forces a player to remove a cube on a spell card such that a box is now empty, the spell is canceled if it has not already occurred. Spells that have already occurred are unaffected. If a spell has already occurred a player may not wound a cube in a box with the wound symbol on it. If a wound forces a player to remove a might cube leaving a dark red (mandatory) box empty, the weapon attack is canceled if it has not already occurred. Attacks that have already occurred are unaffected. When removing cubes, the order of attacks or hit determination may change. Use the new number of cubes to determine the next unresolved attack to occur and the resolution of all subsequent attacks this combat round. Attacks that have already been resolved are unaffected.

title: Monster Death
content: When a monster is killed, the hero who strikes the final blow (or any monster/spell controlled by that hero) takes the monster counter and places it near their hero board. Exception: Elementals are returned to the pool and may be resummoned. The hero immediately receives the fame value printed on the counter.

title: Hero Death
content: When a hero is killed, discard half of the hero’s fame (rounded down). Of the remainder, for each 10 fame the hero can discard, they receive 1 LP. The hero’s lineage and class cards, along with their LPs and left-over fame, are set aside. A dead hero is still eligible to win the game (depending on the scenario being played). Discard all missions and spells from the known spells location on the hero board (return hero starting spell cards to the box). Place the hero’s targeting token in the clearing where they died. Shuffle all of the hero’s possessions and place them,face- down near the board along with all of the hero’s gold (keep spell cards with their spell books and scrolls). Place the hero counter on top of the pile. The hero’s possessions may be searched for and looted like a normal treasure site. When the hero’s body is found, the finder immediately receives all gold on the body, but no LPs or fame. Possessions must be looted.

title: End of Combat
content: When combat is completed, a few things happen: • Discard all pink status cubes from monsters. Monster counters are placed name side up in the clearing. All wounded hearts and cubes in a hero’s wounded box remain there. • If a hero that threw a weapon during any combat round is still in the clearing, and no monsters are in the clearing, that hero retrieves their thrown weapon for free and places it face-down in their backpack. Otherwise, remove the weapon from the game permanently. • Heroes may retire using the rules below. After heroes have had the chance to retire, if it is not the end of the game, continue with the Action Phase of the next turn.

title: Retirement
content: If a hero is in a civilization location at the end of the battle phase, that hero may choose to retire. When a hero retires, the following occurs: • For each 10 fame the hero discards, they receive 1 LP. Remaining fame is kept as a tie-breaker. • If the hero is retiring on the last turn of the game, the hero receives one LP for being a living legend. • Roll two monster dice for each outlaw token the hero possesses (see Outlaw Tokens on page 24). • If both dice show a symbol, the outlaw gains 1 LP. • If one die result is a symbol and the other is a blank, they discard one 1 LP. If they have no LPs, they lose all of their remaining fame. • If both dice show blanks, there is no effect. • Set the LPs, fame, lineage card, and class card for the hero aside and remove the hero’s counter from the map.

title: Starting a New Hero
content: A player that dies or retires may select another hero to begin play on the following turn. The set up for this new hero follows the rules for set up at the beginning of the game. For their starting items search the item deck for the cards and then reshuffle. If the equipment is not available, the hero receives the sale price gold equivalent instead. A spell caster may choose spells from the hero starting spell cards set back in the box earlier. The new hero begins as per the rules of the scenario being played.

title: End of the Game
content: At the end of the game, all surviving heroes retire based on their ending location: • Civilization location: Retire normally following the retirement rules. • Not in a civilization location: The hero loses half, rounded down, of their fame and then retires normally as if they were in a civilization location. Victory is per the rules for the scenario being played.

title: Combat Example
content: The barbarian and knight are unhidden and blocked in a clearing with a Juvenile Dragon, a Giant, and the Great Drake. They are both fully healthy and possess their original starting equipment as listed on the cards shown above. The knight did not alert this turn and is limited to 5 cubes each combat round. The barbarian alerted during the action phase and may play +1 speed cube per combat round. The heroes’ equipped weapons are also shown above.

title: Combat Round 1
content: 1. Challenge: The three monsters all challenge a random hero. After die rolls, the Juvenile Dragon and Giant challenge the knight and the Great Drake challenges the barbarian. 2. Activation: Neither hero is under the effects of a permanent spell so nothing happens during this step. 3. Evade: Neither the knight, nor the barbarian, can play more maneuver cubes than the monsters challenging them so neither of them may evade combat this turn. 4. Target: The monsters each target the heroes they challenged. The barbarian decides to target the Great Drake and the knight decides to target the Juvenile Dragon since it is worth more fame than the Giant. 5. Hero Tactics: Secretly each hero places their cubes on their cards. The barbarian and knight decide to place their cubes as shown below.

title: Combat Example
content: 6. Monster Tactics: One monster die is rolled for each monster. The roll for the Juvenile Dragon and the Great Drake each show a symbol, so they both flip over to their back sides. The roll for the Giant shows a blank, so the Giant does not flip over. The new combat values of the monsters are shown below in order of attack from left to right (note that the two dragons’ attack speeds and attack length (0) are equal so their attacks hit simultaneously. 7. Resolution: The knight’s attack speed equals the attack speed of both dragons, but the attack length of the long sword is higher than the length of the dragons’ attacks (10 vs. 0). The knight will attack first. • The knight’s attack speed (2) is compared to the Juvenile Dragon’s maneuver speed (3). It is not an automatic hit because the attack speed is not higher than the maneuver speed. The knight will have to roll the combat dice and get lucky. The knight rolls the dice and rolls two hit symbols! This is an automatic hit regardless of the maneuver speed of the monster. The damage done is equal to the number of cubes played on the knight’s weapon (2) + 1 sword icon on the weapon. Because the dragon is armored one sword icon is canceled resulting in two actual damage, which is just enough to kill the dragon. The knight places the Juvenile Dragon counter and 10 fame near his hero board. • The Great Drake attacks next with an attack speed of two. The barbarian’s maneuver speed is also two so the hit dice are rolled for the Great Drake. The result is a hit symbol and a tied symbol and, following the golden rule of Dragons Down, only the worse result applies; the tied symbol. Unfortunately for the barbarian, this is enough for the Great Drake to hit since the dragon’s attack speed and the barbarian’s maneuver speed are equal. The barbarian’s helmet is destroyed (the damage of the attack is 4 + 1 sword - 1 sword for the helmet, which is greater than the 2 armor value of the helmet). In addition, the barbarian must immediately wound a cube. The barbarian chooses to place their unused brown speed cube in the wounded box on his hero board. • The Giant attacks next with an attack speed of one, which ties the knight’s maneuver speed. The hit dice are rolled and two blanks are the result. The Giant misses. • The final attack is the barbarian’s attack with an attack speed of zero. All of the barbarian’s effort was put into might since that is needed to kill the Great Drake in one swing. The Great Drake has a maneuver speed of 1, so the barbarian rolls the hit dice. One die shows a hit and one die shows a blank symbol, which means the attack misses. The end of combat round 1 is shown on the next page. The barbarian has lost his helmet (not shown). Two monsters remain.

title: Combat Round 2
content: 1. Challenge: Both monsters randomly challenge the knight in the combat round. This means the barbarian will not be targeted this round and can put all of her efforts into attacking her target without fear of being attacked. 2. Activation: Nothing happens. 3. Evade: Neither hero evades. 4. Target: Both monsters target the knight. The knight decides to attack the Giant and the barbarian decides to target the Great Drake again. 5. Hero Tactics: Secretly each hero places their cubes on their cards. The barbarian and knight decide to place all their brown cubes in attack speed. 6. Monster Tactics: One monster die is rolled for each monster and neither roll shows a symbol so the monsters remain in their same tactics. 7. Resolution: The knight’s attack again goes first. • The knight’s attack speed (3) is higher than the Giant’s maneuver speed (1) and does 3 actual damage because the Giant is not armored. The Giant is killed. The knight takes the Giant counter and 8 more fame. • The barbarian’s attack is next and is faster than the Great Drake’s maneuver speed (2 vs. 1). The damage done is 4 (4 + 1 sword - 1 for armor) which is just enough to kill the Great Drake. The barbarian takes the Great Drake counter and 20 fame! Combat round 2 ends with no more monsters in the clearing and combat ends.

title: Statuses
content: There are four status effects tracked on a player’s hero board: alert, sneak, make noise, and hidden. Hidden status is explained below and all others are explained under their respective sections in the Action Phase rules. All statuses are reset at the beginning of each turn by removing all pink status cubes from hero boards.

title: Hidden Status
content: When a player makes a successful hide reaction, the player places a pink cube in the hidden box on the hero’s hero board to signify that the hero is hidden.

title: Action Phase
content: Hidden heroes may take actions in the clearing as normal, including when a hide attempt is successful in the middle of their turn. Heroes lose their hidden status if they move to a new clearing or take the make noise action. Heroes may voluntarily reveal themselves at any time during the action phase.

title: Battle Phase
content: During the battle phase, heroes may voluntarily reveal themselves only at the beginning of the challenge step of a combat round. Hidden heroes may not be attacked, but may ambush using spells or ranged weapons (see Combat, page 15).

title: Treasures and Items
content: Dragons Down is a land full of powerful relics that can greatly enhance your hero. The abilities of each treasure or item are shown via iconography in the bottom half of the card. Until you get to know the iconography, you can use the alphabetical treasure manifest in the appendix of these rules to understand each treasure.

title: Items
content: Heroes begin the game with various equipment specific to the hero’s class as listed on the card. Item cards have the word “Item” on the back of the card and have a wooden banner on the front of the card. The layout for item cards are identical to treasure cards.

title: Deep Treasures vs. Treasures
content: Some treasures are found deeper in the treasure sites that heroes will loot and are known as deep treasures. Deep treasures are the same as treasures, but tend to be more valuable, and contain a higher percentage of epic treasures (see below).

title: Epic Treasures
content: Treasures that have a brown banner on them are regular treasures. These are the normal treasures one would find in a treasure site. Treasures that have a red game permanently if all monsters are not killed during combat this turn. banner are epic treasures. These are the treasures about which legends and stories are told. They are the best treasures in the game and earn legend points and fame for whomever reveals them. When an epic treasure card (with a red banner) is revealed for the first time, the revealing player earns LPs and fame as indicated on the player reference card. Rewards for epic treasures only occur once per game per epic treasure.

title: Treasure and Item Banners
content: The banners on treasures and items show information as follows: Base Price: This is the price that a merchant will pay to purchase this card from a hero. This is also the base price used to calculate how much a merchant will charge to sell this card to a hero (the price is always base price x3) One-time Use: This card is removed from the game after use. One- time use cards may be used at any time during a player’s turn or in combat, even when first possessed without equipping. Cards with a combat effect may only be used in combat. Armor: This card is armor with an armor value as printed in the shield symbol. Armor is explained in the combat section on page 16 of these rules. Weight: This card requires that a hero has a number of healthy might cubes equal to the number shown. If not at any time, the card is immediately unequipped to the hero’s backpack (see Equipping on page 21). Attack Length: If two attacks have the same attack speed, weapons and spells with higher numbers are resolved before lower numbers. Some weapons have two numbers. See Melee or Ranged below. Melee: This card is a melee weapon. Ranged: This card is a ranged weapon. If it hits, roll the ranged attack dice to modify the effects of the attack as described in the combat section of these rules. Melee or Ranged: This weapon may be used as a melee or a ranged weapon. If used as a melee weapon, use the top attack length. If used as a ranged weapon (thrown), use the bottom attack length. Weapons may only be thrown with one hand. When thrown, they are placed to the side of the hero board. Thrown weapons are removed from the Permanent: The effects of this magic item last for the entire game. Combat: The effects of this treasure last for the duration of the combat. Once combat is over, the effects are terminated. Position Neck: This card is placed on the hero’s neck when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Position Waist: This card is placed on the hero’s waist when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Position Feet: This card is placed on the hero’s feet when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Position Head: This card is placed on the hero’s head when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Position Chest: This card is placed on the hero’s chest when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Position Head and Chest: This card is placed on the hero’s head and chest when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Place the card on the white dotted lined area that covers both locations. Neither location is available for other cards. Position One-handed Weapon: This card is placed on one of the hero’s weapon locations (does not matter which one) when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). A hero may not have two weapons active, even if both are one-handed weapons. Position Two-handed Weapon: This card is placed on both of the hero’s weapon locations when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Place the card on the white dotted lined area that covers both locations. Neither location is available for other cards. Spears may be wielded with one or two-hands. The optional might box is only available if using two hands. Position Single Hand: This card is placed on one of the hero’s hand locations (does not matter which one) when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Position Two Hands: This card is placed on both of the hero’s hand locations when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Place the card on the white dotted lined area that covers both locations. Neither location is available for other cards. Position Miscellaneous: This card is placed on one of the hero’s miscellaneous locations (does not matter which one) when active (and face-down in the backpack when inactive). Position Backpack: Cards may always be placed in the backpack. Cards placed in the backpack are face-down, inactive, hidden from other players, and need not be revealed. Position Backpack Special: This card must always be face-up. If face- down and viewed by a hero, it becomes active and is placed face-up (treasure pile, merchant, etc.). If its owner is killed, it is placed face-up in the clearing. Anyone entering the clearing immediately takes possession of the card. Instantaneous: The effects of this treasure occur immediately. The treasure is then removed from the game.

title: Equipping
content: Treasures and items may be either unequipped (face-down in the hero’s backpack on their hero board) or equipped (face-up in any matching location on the hero’s hero board). Heroes only receive the benefit of equipped treasures unless otherwise noted on the treasure card. Unequipped treasures have no impact on the game and are kept face-down in the backpack. Exception: Position Backpack Special above. Equipping is the process of moving item and treasure cards to and from various locations on your hero board. Equipping follows these rules: • Equipping is placing a card face-up on a location that matches the location symbol on the card. A card may only be placed on a location that matches the symbol on the card or in your backpack. Unequipping is placing a card face-down in your backpack. Exception: • Cards with a red location symbol are always placed face-up. • When a hero gains possession of a new item or treasure card, they must immediately choose to equip it or unequip it. • If they choose to equip the card, they unequip any card(s) already in that location. They may not equip other cards, nor unequip cards not in the location in which they are equipping the new card. • Heroes may not equip more than one weapon in their weapon locations. • Heroes can gain possession of new items or treasures in many ways, including the loot action, the trade action, and by revealing an item or treasure token in a tile after movement. • Weight: Armor has a weight as shown by the number on a red cube icon on the armor card. Weapons have a weight equal to the number of dark red/mandatory boxes on the card. A hero may not equip armor unless they possess at least as many healthy might cubes as the weight of the individual armor. A hero may not equip a weapon card unless they can fill all open dark red/mandatory boxes. If, at any time, a hero does not have enough healthy cubes for the weight of an armor or weapon, it is immediately unequipped to their backpack, even during combat. • During the Adjust Equipment step of combat, a hero that did not place any cubes on weapons or spells in the combat round may unequip one card and equip one card. This card may be the same card. • During the Rearm step, a hero that threw a melee/ranged weapon may equip one card from their backpack to a weapon location. • During an alert action, a hero may freely equip and unequip any cards. • Missions are also stored in a hero’s backpack for easy reference, but mission cards are never equipped or unequipped. • All face-up cards are public knowledge. All face-down cards are not public knowledge, but a hero may look at all cards in their backpack at any time.

title: Haggling
content: A hero may haggle with a merchant over the price of a card they are trying to buy during a trade action. Place the card being haggled over apart from the merchant’s other cards so as to avoid confusion over which card is involved (a player may choose to place the card face-up or keep it secret while haggling). Each merchant has an attribute icon that they respect printed next to their name on the terrain setup cards. The haggle number the hero needs to roll to successfully haggle is the sum of the number of matching attribute icons on the hero’s lineage and class cards. If the hero possesses one or more outlaw tokens, the hero suffers a penalty of -1 icon when haggling with a merchant that respects only wisdom and receives a bonus of +1 icon when haggling with a merchant that respects only cunning. The number of outlaw tokens does not matter. The minimum haggle number is 0. The haggling hero rolls two haggle dice: • If either die shows a closed door, the haggle attempt fails and the merchant closes their doors to the hero for the rest of the turn. No more trade attempts may be made with that merchant by that hero until the following turn. • If the highest number rolled is higher than the haggle number, the haggle attempt fails and the trade action is terminated. The hero may attempt to trade and haggle with the merchant using subsequent actions, if they wish. • If the highest number rolled is less than or equal to the haggle number, the haggle attempt is a success. The price to purchase the card during this trade action is reduced by a factor of one (from 3x to 2x or from 2x to 1x). The hero may continue haggling as part of the same trade action, if they wish. The price of a card will never be reduced below 1x. If the card is not purchased for any reason, return the card to the merchant.

title: Natives
content: Natives represent the various civilized people that have moved back into the realm. Natives are placed at the civilization location listed on the terrain setup card. Natives do not block or attack heroes. Natives can be targeted like a monster. If any native is targeted during combat, the following occurs: • All natives in the clearing are treated as monsters for all purposes during combat this turn. • At the end of the targeting step, each native in the clearing that is not already targeting a hero targets a random hero that targeted a native this turn, even if not targeting a native this combat round. Once combat is complete in the clearing, natives return to their prior behavior.

title: Undead
content: Some monsters are undead as indicated by their health value being printed on top of a skull on their monster token. Undead monsters have invulnerability to some spells, and weaknesses towards other spells (both are indicated on the individual spell cards either in text or by a special symbol indicating that it does not affect the undead). In all other ways, undead behave like normal monsters.

title: Spells
content: Dragons Down is a world full of magic. One way that heroes access this magic is via spells. There are two decks of spell cards. One deck, labeled “Hero Starting Spell”, is used only when a player creates a hero and selects their starting spells. Do not shuffle this deck. Once heroes have selected their starting spells, this deck is set aside and not used in this game session. The setup of the other deck, labeled “Spell”, is described in the setup procedures of these rules. Heroes may cast spells using the cards of either deck. Heroes may learn the same spell from each deck. Spells are only cast during combat. Spells may be cast each battle phase even if no monsters are present in a clearing. If the hero was hidden when the spell was cast, they must attempt a hide reaction to remain hidden. This hide attempt may not be modified by the sneak action or the halfling ability. To cast a spell, take magic cubes from the healthy area of your hero board, and cover all boxes on the spell card with matching colors. If you cannot cover all the boxes, you cannot cast the spell. Exception: if the hero is in an enchanted tile, they may ignore any one spell box that matches the color of the tile’s enchantment cube. You may only cast one spell per combat round. Spells that have a duration longer than instantaneous may not be cast again until the spell is broken or expires. Note: Each spell box type is differentiated by a unique color and symbol. The tapestry on each spell card shows the spells characteristics as follows: Price: The base price of the spell card. Spell cards cannot be bought or sold unless attached to a spell book or spell scroll. When a hero buys or sells a spell book or spell scroll, all spells remain attached to the treasure card. The base price of a spell book or spell scroll is the sum of the spells attached to the treasure card (see page 29 for more information on spell books and spell scrolls). Targeted: This spell must be targeted at the caster or a single target in the clearing with the caster. If there is a number in the target symbol, the caster may target up to that many targets. The spell only takes effect if the spell hits using normal attack rules. A hero may voluntarily accept a hit from a targeted spell when cast. Self or other: This spell may be cast on self, another hero, or a monster in the same clearing as the caster. The spell does not need to hit to take effect. Self: This spell targets the caster and automatically takes effect when cast. Melee: The casting of this spell acts like a melee weapon. If it hits, treat it like a melee weapon attack per the explanation on the card. Ranged: The casting of this spell acts like a ranged weapon. If it hits, roll the ranged attack dice to modify the effects of the attack as normal. Instantaneous: The spell occurs instantly and then expires. Combat: The spell lasts for the duration of combat, until the caster or target is killed or evades. Then the spell expires.
